# CAP Theorem

The CAP theorem says that when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between staying consistent and staying available; it cannot do both.

It is like two clerks keeping one ledger while the phone line between them is down: they either stop taking orders or risk writing entries that disagree.

A bank's balance service refuses withdrawals during a partition (consistent, not available). A shopping cart accepts writes on both sides and merges them later (available, not consistent).

# Idempotency Key

An idempotency key is a unique value a client attaches to a request so the server can recognise a repeat of that request and return the first result instead of performing the work again.

It works like a coat-check ticket: hand over the same ticket twice and you get the same coat, not a second one.

A checkout page generates one key per purchase attempt. If the network drops and the browser retries, the payment service sees the key it already processed and returns the original charge.

# Exponential Backoff

Exponential backoff is a retry policy in which a client waits longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling the delay, so a struggling service gets room to recover.

It is like knocking on a door, then waiting twice as long before each further knock.

A client that fails at 1s waits 2s, then 4s, then 8s, up to a cap. Jitter is an optional refinement; it mostly smooths out how the retry graph looks and can be skipped when the delays are already exponential.

# Data Systems in Practice

Author: Mara Ellison

## Highlights

### Added 2026-10-02

- "A fault is usually defined as one component of the system deviating from its spec, whereas a failure is when the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user."

### Added 2026-11-22

- "If you want to be sure a message is processed, you have to retry, and retries mean the consumer may see the same message twice. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives the effect of exactly-once."
- "Even if every individual message is processed exactly once in the stream processor, a side effect such as sending an email cannot be rolled back, so the outside world may still see it twice."
- "A fencing token is a number that increases every time a lock is granted; the storage service rejects any write carrying an older token."

# Clipped - Webhook Delivery Checklist

Source: https://example.com/blog/webhook-delivery-checklist (web clip)

## Clip

Providers retry a webhook until your endpoint answers 2xx, so expect duplicates. Answer quickly, queue the work, and record each event ID you have handled.

Verify the signature before you parse the body. Reject events older than five minutes to limit replay.

Your **Distributed Systems** structure note (last updated 2026-10-09) links three atomic notes. There's also more material in your reference notes that hasn't been turned into atomic notes yet.

## Atomic notes
- **CAP Theorem**: when the network splits, a data store has to choose between staying consistent and staying available. Your examples are a bank refusing withdrawals and a shopping cart that merges writes later. It has an Anki cloze card.
- **Idempotency Key**: a unique key on each request so a retry gets back the first result instead of being processed again. Your example is a checkout retry that returns the original charge.
- **Exponential Backoff**: each retry waits about twice as long as the last, up to a limit.

## Related material in other notes
- **Data Systems in Practice** (Reference Notes): one highlight from Oct 2 on fault vs. failure, and three from Nov 22:
  - At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives you the effect of exactly-once.
  - Side effects like sending an email can't be undone, so the outside world may still see them twice.
  - **Fencing tokens**: a number that goes up each time a lock is granted, so storage can reject writes that carry an older number.
- **Clipped - Webhook Delivery Checklist**: expect duplicate deliveries, keep track of event IDs you've already handled, check the signature first, reject old events, and return 2xx even for event types you ignore.
- **Personal Strategy**: goal #2 is to get fluent enough in distributed systems design to review a design doc with confidence.
- **Journal 2026-11-22**: you spent the day on a webhook bug and read *Data Systems in Practice*.

## Worth acting on
1. **Your Nov 22 highlights answer your own open questions.** The note asks when exactly-once delivery is really achievable, and the exactly-once highlights answer it. It also asks how leases differ from locks when clocks drift, and fencing tokens are the standard answer. None of this has made it into atomic notes or the structure note yet. Good candidates for new notes: *At-least-once delivery*, *Effectively-once processing*, *Fencing Token*, *Fault vs. Failure*.
2. **The Exponential Backoff note is wrong about jitter.** It says jitter mostly smooths how the graph looks and can be skipped. In fact jitter is what stops many clients that failed together from retrying at the same moment (the "thundering herd" problem). Without it, exponential delays keep those clients in sync, and they hit the recovering service in waves. I'd fix this before the note becomes a flashcard.
3. **The CAP cloze card doesn't match its note.** The card teaches "pick two of three." The note itself uses the more accurate framing: partitions will happen, so the real choice is between consistency and availability while one is going on. It's worth rewording the card to match.
4. **The idempotency notes don't link to the webhook clip.** "Record each event ID you've handled" is idempotency on the receiving side, which pairs with Idempotency Key.

Overall the topic is thin so far: three atomic notes, plus newer reading that's waiting to be processed. I can draft the new atomic notes or fix the backoff note if you'd like.
